newsitem.title: UK: Spice Girls and soap open new British tv channel.
newsitem.headline: Spice Girls and soap open new British tv channel.

text.p: The first new British terrestrial television channel in 15 years opened on Sunday with a theme tune sung by the Spice Girls and a soap opera that attracted complaints even before it was broadcast.
Channel 5 is hoping to hook viewers by showing a half-hour soap, Family Affairs, AT 6.30 each evening.
But Conservative lawmaker Nicholas Winterton complained in advance after hearing of one scene in the opening episode in which a tattoo is exposed on a man's buttock.
"It is unacceptable to have nude scenes on at a time when children are watching," Winterton said.

The top-selling Spice Girls' theme tune -- a reworked version of Manfred Mann's 1964 hit "5-4-3-2-1" -- claimed Channel 5 was "guaranteed to be a new sensation", and the introductory half-hour programme vowed it would be modern and fast-moving.
"A lot of people under 50 are just not watching the news," said news reader Kirsty Young, 28, who promised that Channel 5 news would be "more exciting to make it accessible".
It would "not simply be a man in a suit sitting behind a desk", she added.
The Channel will have a half-hour news programme at 2030 each night and a bulletin on the hour, except during the film slot between 2100 and 2300 each weekday evening.
The station has trumpeted Hollywood blockbusters like "Independence Day" although the first night offering was a home-grown true-life drama about an abducted estate agent.
Earlier, it showed a documentary about the early life of Prime Minister John Major and Tony Blair, the Labour leader who looks set to steal his job after the May 1 election.
Channel 5 is owned by British media groups Pearson Plc and United News & Media plus European broadcaster CLT-Ufa and U.S. investment firm Warburg Pincus.

It has a core programme budget of just 110 million pounds ($179.6 million) compared with ITV's 600 million and had to find 150 million pounds -- three times more than planned -- even before it went on the air to hire an army of technicians to retune millions of video recorders affected by interference from its signal.
